one_liner: Single-kernel CUDA SPHINCS+-SHA256-f-simple batch signer/verifier; 1.37-3.45x over Kim et al.'s GPU code, 1,820-3,659x the single-core reference.
what_it_does: GRASP (IEEE Transactions on Computers 2026; ePrint 2024/1030) is a CUDA implementation of round-3 SPHINCS+ signing and verification for server-side batches. It is measured only on the SHA-256 'simple' fast parameter sets (128f/192f/256f). In the throughput mode, a small team of threads (11 at levels 1 and 3, 18 at level 5) computes each signature inside one fused kernel, and each verification runs on one thread. A separate low-latency signing mode spreads one signature over thousands of threads (6,160 for WOTS+ key generation at level 1). No code, API or build instructions were released, so there is no interface to adopt.
how_it_is_fast: Kernel fusion runs FORS, WOTS+ and the MSS hypertree in a single CUDA kernel. This avoids the global-memory hand-offs of Kim et al.'s multi-kernel design. The thread-team size is chosen so that both the hypertree layer count d and the FORS tree count k divide evenly (gcd(22,33)=11), with one thread per layer or subtree, so no threads sit idle during node merging. When the root of the layer below is already known, WOTS+ signing is folded into that leaf's public-key chain computation, which removes about 33% of the hash calls for those leaves and cuts separate WOTS+ signings from d to t per thread. The n-byte hash blocks move with 16-byte int4 loads and stores at levels 1 and 5, and with int2 at level 3, where 24-byte blocks would misalign.
when_to_use: High-volume SPHINCS+ signing on a data-center GPU (e.g. a code- or firmware-signing farm) that accepts SHA-256 fast-simple parameters: 146,363 / 82,621 / 40,489 signatures/s at levels 1/3/5 on an RTX 4090.
Mass verification of SPHINCS+-SHA256-f signatures: 1.5M/s at level 1 on an RTX 4090, one thread per signature.
A GPU signer that needs per-signature latency: the low-latency mode signs in 0.512 ms at level 1 (25 ms for the CPU reference, 4.8 ms for Kim et al.), at the cost of dropping to 19,521 ops/s.

Reference techniques for your own GPU or CPU hash-based signer. Kernel fusion, gcd-sized thread teams and merging WOTS+ signing into leaf keygen are all described in enough detail to reimplement, and the paper says the WOTS+ merge also helps CPU code.
when_not_to_use: You need code. None was released and there is no license. The only open GPU SPHINCS+ code found is Kim et al.'s kindongsy/TCAS-SPHINCSp_GPU, which is unlicensed and consists of per-security-level Visual Studio projects.
You need SHAKE, Haraka, 'robust' or small (s) parameter sets. Only SHA-256 fast-simple was measured; the claim that it is 'equally effective in all modes' is asserted, not benchmarked.
You need FIPS 205 SLH-DSA compliance. The work targets SPHINCS+ round 3 (reference code v3.0), and compatibility with the final SLH-DSA standard is not documented.
Small batches in the throughput mode. The peak needs a 128x512 grid; at 128x64, level-1 signing drops to 66.4 kops/s, 45% of the peak.

Sizing end-to-end PCIe throughput from the headline. It excludes host-device copies: with memcpy, RTX 4090 level-1 signing falls from 146,363 to 117,723 ops/s, and with-memcpy verification numbers are not reported.

integration.form: not released (paper only; described as one fused CUDA kernel for signing and one for verification)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented: the paper says only 'NVCC compiler' on Linux, with no CUDA version or flags
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs: measured on RTX 4090, RTX 3090 and GTX 1080 under Linux

gotchas: Level-3 verification is reported inconsistently: the text says 1,408,846 ops/s, while Table VI and Fig. 13 say 933,696 (933.7 kops/s). The table value drives the 1897.76x and 1.80x ratios.

The 1,820-3,659x ratios are against the portable reference C code on one Ryzen 5 5600G core with unstated flags (40/26/13 sign/s, 739/492/487 verify/s). No optimized CPU SPHINCS+ implementation was compared.

The gap over Kim et al. shrinks with apples-to-apples conditions: 1.37/1.79/1.58x kernel-only on an RTX 4090 (Kim's open-source code re-run), 1.36/1.65/1.49x with memcpy, and 1.22/1.25/1.30x on an RTX 3090 against Kim's published with-memcpy figures.
The low-latency and high-throughput modes are separate thread configurations. Low-latency gives 5.5x lower throughput than Kim et al. on the RTX 4090, so pick one per deployment.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick GRASP when you are committed to hash-based SPHINCS+ signatures and need GPU batch throughput. GOLF is the same group's GPU design for Falcon; it reaches 420k sign/s on the same RTX 4090 with 666-byte Falcon-512 signatures versus 17,088 bytes for SPHINCS+-128f, and it also ships no code. The CPU siblings (VecFalcon, ENG25519, UltrafastSecp256k1) release code and suit per-signature latency on CPUs.
verified_claims_summary: On an RTX 4090, timing kernels only (host-device copies excluded, averaged over 1,000 runs, NVCC version and flags unstated), GRASP signs 146,363 / 82,621 / 40,489 and verifies 1,499,590 / 933,696 / 886,362 SPHINCS+-SHA256-128f/192f/256f-simple signatures per second. That is 3,114-3,659x (signing) and 1,820-2,029x (verification) the NIST reference C code v3.0 on one Ryzen 5 5600G core. The like-for-like result is 1.37-1.79x signing and 1.53-3.45x verification over Kim et al.'s open-source GPU code re-run on the same RTX 4090.
status_note: This is unreleased research code from a peer-reviewed paper (IEEE TC vol. 75 no. 4, pp. 1579-1592, 2026; ePrint revised 2025-01-16) with no repo, license or maintenance, so treat it as a technique reference only. Both the ePrint and the journal version are titled 'GRASP: Accelerating Hash-based PQC Performance on GPU Parallel Architecture'; the catalog name is the expanded acronym.
